title: Access Token Manipulation: SID-History Injection
summary: SID-History injection abuses a directory attribute that exists so accounts can migrate between domains without losing access. A Windows security identifier, or SID, is the value that access checks actually compare, and every token carries the account SID plus the SIDs of its groups. The SID-History attribute on a directory account holds additional SIDs that are folded into the token at logon, so a trusted domain can keep honouring old identifiers. An attacker holding domain administrator rights can append a well-known or harvested SID, such as a built in privileged group or an enterprise administrator value from another domain, to an account they control. The result is an ordinary account whose token contains extraordinary membership, which unlocks local resources and trusted domain resources without any group membership change. Detection rests on the attribute itself: directory changes to SID-History are rare and almost always administrative, so any modification should be compared against a change record, and the follow on evidence is a token that carries a privileged SID for an account whose group list does not justify it.

beginner.definition: A security identifier, short for SID, is the unique code Windows uses for a user or group, like an account number. Some accounts can carry extra SIDs in a list called SID-History, which exists to help when accounts move between domains. An attacker can add powerful SIDs to that list so the account is treated as more important than it really is.
beginner.whyItMatters: Access is decided by these codes, not by names shown on screen. If you add a powerful code to a small account, that account opens doors it should never touch. Group membership reports look normal, so routine reviews find nothing. Only watching the directory attribute itself reveals the change.
howItWorks: A SID is a unique code that Windows checks whenever it decides access to a resource.
Access tokens hold the account SID and the SIDs of the groups it belongs to.
The SID-History attribute holds extra SIDs, and all of them are added to the token at logon.
An attacker with domain administrator rights edits the attribute on an account they control.
They insert a privileged SID, so the token carries rights that no group list shows.
The account can then reach local files and other trusted domains by remote connections.
beginner.example: Imagine a border checkpoint where officers trust the stamps inside your passport. A clerk with access to the stamp drawer adds a diplomatic stamp to an ordinary passport. The passport itself is genuine and the photo matches. At every later checkpoint the officers see the diplomatic stamp and wave the traveller past, because the stamp drawer record is the only place the change appears.
takeaways: SIDs are what access checks use, so SID-History can grant rights without group membership.
Changes to SID-History are rare, so any change deserves a review against a valid reason.
Keep domain administrator rights few and monitored, because this abuse needs them.

objectives: Explain what a Windows security identifier is and how it is used in access checks.
Describe the legitimate purpose of the SID-History attribute and what it does to logon tokens.
Explain what rights an attacker needs before this injection is possible.
Identify the directory change that reveals SID-History tampering and where it is logged.
Explain how injected SIDs enable access to other domains through remote services.
